questions.question: A fraction bar the length of one whole is cut into 2 equal parts and 1 part is shaded. A second bar of exactly the same length is cut into 6 equal parts and 1 part is shaded. Altogether, what fraction of one whole bar is shaded, in lowest terms?
questions.explain: Rewrite 1/2 as 3/6 so both bars have parts of the same size, then 3/6 + 1/6 = 4/6, which reduces to 2/3. The classic trap is adding the denominators too and getting 2/8 — the denominator only tells you the size of the parts, so it never gets added.

questions.question: A fraction bar the length of one whole is cut into 3 equal parts and 2 parts are shaded. A second bar of the same length is cut into 6 equal parts and 1 part is shaded. How much more of the first bar is shaded than the second, in lowest terms?
questions.explain: Sixths are the common size here, so 2/3 becomes 4/6 and 4/6 − 1/6 = 3/6 = 1/2. Subtracting the bottoms as well (giving 1/3) is the usual slip — you can only subtract parts that are the same size.

questions.question: A fraction bar the length of one whole is cut into 4 equal parts and 1 part is shaded. A second bar of the same length is cut into 12 equal parts and 1 part is shaded. What fraction of one whole bar is shaded in total, in lowest terms?
questions.explain: Twelfths are the common size, and 1/4 is the same as 3/12, so 3/12 + 1/12 = 4/12 = 1/3. Writing 1/12 + 1/12 = 2/12 is the trap: when the denominator is multiplied by 3, the numerator must be multiplied by 3 as well.

questions.question: A fraction bar the length of one whole is cut into 8 equal parts and 7 parts are shaded. A second bar of the same length is cut into 4 equal parts and 1 part is shaded. How much more of the first bar is shaded than the second, in lowest terms?
questions.explain: Change 1/4 into 2/8 so both amounts are counted in eighths, then 7/8 − 2/8 = 5/8. Leaving 1/4 as 1/8 and getting 6/8 is the common error — changing the bottom number always changes the top number too.

questions.question: Work out 2/5 + 3/10 and give the answer in lowest terms.
questions.explain: Ten is a multiple of 5, so 2/5 becomes 4/10 and 4/10 + 3/10 = 7/10. Adding straight across to get 5/15 is the trap: only the numerators are added once the parts are the same size.

questions.question: Devon walks 3/4 km from home to the SkyTrain station, then 1/6 km from the station to school. How far does Devon walk in total, in lowest terms?
questions.explain: The lowest common denominator of 4 and 6 is 12, so 3/4 + 1/6 becomes 9/12 + 2/12 = 11/12 km. Watch out for 4/12 — that comes from swapping the denominators to 12 but forgetting to scale 3 up to 9 and 1 up to 2.

questions.question: Ava picks 7/10 kg of blueberries and uses 1/5 kg of them for muffins. How many kilograms of blueberries are left, in lowest terms?
questions.explain: Rename 1/5 as 2/10, then 7/10 − 2/10 = 5/10, which must be reduced to 1/2 kg. Stopping at 5/10 is the most common miss — always check whether the top and bottom share a factor.

questions.question: Kai adds 1/2 L of apple juice to 3/8 L of soda water and uses 8 as the common denominator. Which line shows the correct rewriting and the finished answer in lowest terms?
questions.explain: Since 2 × 4 = 8, the numerator of 1/2 is also multiplied by 4, giving 4/8, and 4/8 + 3/8 = 7/8 L. The line starting with 1/8 shows the usual error: the denominator was changed but the numerator was left alone.

questions.question: Owen opens a 1 L carton of milk. He pours 1/2 L into pancake batter and later pours 1/8 L onto his cereal. How much milk is left in the carton, in lowest terms?
questions.explain: First add what he poured: 4/8 + 1/8 = 5/8 L, then subtract from the whole, 8/8 − 5/8 = 3/8 L. The trap is treating 1/2 as 1/8 when changing denominators, which wrongly leaves 6/8 L.

questions.question: Salma needs 3/4 L of stock for her soup. She finds 1/3 L in one jar and 1/4 L in another. How much more stock does she still need, in lowest terms?
questions.explain: She has 4/12 + 3/12 = 7/12 L, and she needs 9/12 L, so 9/12 − 7/12 = 2/12 = 1/6 L. Two things trip students here: scaling the numerators when moving to twelfths, and reducing 2/12 at the end.

questions.question: Priya is working out 2/3 + 1/6. She writes 2/6 + 1/6 = 3/6. What is the best explanation of what went wrong?
options: She should add the tops and the bottoms together, which gives 3/9 as the sum.
Her steps are fine, but 3/6 still needs writing in lowest terms as 1/2.
She kept the numerator 2 when 3 became 6; it should be 4/6 + 1/6 = 5/6.
She should have used 18 as the common denominator: 2/18 + 1/18 = 3/18.
questions.explain: Multiplying the denominator 3 by 2 means multiplying the numerator 2 by 2 as well, so 2/3 = 4/6 and the sum is 5/6. An equivalent fraction keeps the same value only when both numbers are scaled by the same factor.

questions.question: At a school picnic there are two identical trays of veggie sticks. Students eat 5/8 of the first tray and 3/4 of the second. How much is eaten in total, written as a mixed number in lowest terms?
questions.explain: Rename 3/4 as 6/8, add to get 5/8 + 6/8 = 11/8, then rewrite the improper fraction as 1 3/8 trays. Getting exactly 1 tray means 3/4 was copied as 3/8, which shrinks the second amount instead of renaming it.
